screens.title: The Iterator Pattern: Traversing Collections
screens.subtitle: Access elements sequentially without revealing how they are stored

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn a simple but powerful idea: let an iterator handle the steps of traversal so client code never needs to know how a collection stores elements. The Iterator pattern separates traversal from storage, so you can change internal representations without changing consumers. That separation is central to the Java Collections Framework: the Iterator and Iterable interfaces provide a standard contract for moving through lists, sets, trees, or your own custom structures. We'll look at the two roles in the pattern — the aggregate that creates an iterator, and the iterator that walks the elements — and then implement a concrete example with a small library. Along the way you'll see how the enhanced for-loop is simply syntactic sugar over Iterable, why modifying a collection during iteration can raise a ConcurrentModificationException, and where custom iterators let you offer filtered or reverse traversals. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to design a focused iterator for a custom structure and choose safe, maintainable traversal strategies. Consider what collection you use today and how an iterator could free your client code from implementation details.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: An Iterator gives sequential access to elements while keeping the underlying collection private, enabling flexible traversal and loose coupling.

content.html:

Why it matters

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will perform four concrete skills with confidence. First, you will state the fundamental problem the Iterator pattern solves: how to traverse an aggregate without exposing its internal layout. That understanding helps you spot where tight coupling exists. Second, you will implement the Iterator pattern in Java, distinguishing external iterators that the client drives using hasNext and next from Java's Iterable that supports the enhanced for-loop. You'll work with the actual Iterator interface methods and a simple concrete iterator. Third, you will analyze how iterators decouple traversal logic from data storage so client code remains flexible, allowing multiple traversal strategies. Fourth, you will identify scenarios that benefit from custom iterators — for example reverse traversal, filtered iteration, or safe removals — and explain trade-offs such as fail-fast behavior and thread-safety. These objectives prepare you to write maintainable collection code and to choose iterator strategies that reduce coupling in real Java applications.

keyIdea.text: Understand, implement, analyze, and identify appropriate iterator usages in Java to create flexible traversal strategies.

screens.title: Skills and checks
screens.subtitle: Concrete skills, safety checks, and common pitfalls

narration.text: Let's make the objectives actionable with safety checks and common pitfalls to watch for. You should be able to implement an iterator that safely throws NoSuchElementException when you call next beyond the end, and to decide when to implement remove or to throw UnsupportedOperationException. You will learn how Java's iterators are often fail-fast: they detect external structural changes and throw ConcurrentModificationException. That behavior is valuable for catching bugs, but you will also learn when to use concurrent collections or synchronization for multi-threaded access. Finally, you'll practice designing iterators that remain simple — keep traversal logic in the iterator and data manipulation in the aggregate. These checks will help you write maintainable iterators and avoid exposing internal arrays or links directly through getters. Practicing these skills with the provided lab exercises will make the pattern a reliable tool in your Java toolkit.

keyIdea.title: Safety & practice
keyIdea.text: Practice throwing NoSuchElementException, decide on remove semantics, and understand fail-fast versus thread-safe iteration.

  • remove can be supported or throw UnsupportedOperationException — decide based on aggregate capabilities.
  • Fail-fast iterators detect structural modification and surface bugs early with ConcurrentModificationException.
  • For multi-threaded access, prefer concurrent collections or synchronize iteration and modification.
Practice tips
Keep iterator state minimal: a reference to the aggregate and a position index or node reference. Delegate complex removals or rebalancing to the aggregate. Keep iterators focused on traversal and element access.

screens.title: Problem: Traversal without exposing structure
screens.subtitle: Why clients shouldn't need to know how collections store data

narration.text: When code that uses a collection depends on the collection's internal layout, it becomes brittle. Imagine a client that iterates by indexing into an array and then the aggregate switches to a linked list. That client must be rewritten. The Iterator pattern addresses this by providing a traversal object with a small interface: check if more elements exist and obtain the next element. The aggregate still controls storage, but it also provides a factory method to produce an iterator. A concrete iterator knows how to walk the aggregate without exposing implementation details. A concrete example is a Library class that keeps books in an array internally but returns a LibraryIterator. The client only calls hasNext and next. This pattern reduces coupling, centralizes traversal logic, and permits multiple traversal strategies — forward, reverse, or filtered — without changing clients. A common mistake is to return the internal array or expose nodes directly; avoid that. Practice the thought experiment: how would a client change if the underlying storage switched from array to linked nodes? If the client remains identical, your iterator design succeeded.

keyIdea.title: Problem summary
keyIdea.text: Tightly coupled traversal forces client changes when storage changes. Iterators preserve client stability by encapsulating traversal.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Traversal Problem
Definition
Provide sequential access to elements without revealing internal structure

When client code knows internal details, maintenance is hard. Encapsulating traversal prevents wide-reaching changes when internals change.

  • Encapsulation: aggregate keeps storage private.
  • Traversal object: iterator exposes a simple contract for stepping through elements.
  • Multiple strategies: return different iterators for different orders or filters.
Analogy
Think of the iterator as a remote control for reading pages from a book collection. The remote moves you page-by-page without opening the box that stores the books.
Example scenario
A Library uses an array today and later switches to a linked structure. If clients use iterators, they continue to work unchanged.
Key takeaway
Design iterators to keep traversal detail in one place so you can evolve data structures safely.

screens.title: Iterator and Aggregate: the two roles
screens.subtitle: Interface contracts and the concrete partners that implement them

narration.text: The Iterator pattern revolves around two cooperating roles: the Iterator and the Aggregate. The Iterator role declares the operations for walking a collection: commonly hasNext to check for more elements and next to retrieve the next element. Some iterators also provide remove to delete the current element safely. The Aggregate role declares a factory method that returns an iterator instance—often called createIterator or iterator. Concrete implementations pair these roles: a Concrete Aggregate stores elements and returns a Concrete Iterator configured to traverse that storage. The Concrete Iterator holds a reference to the aggregate and internal state such as an index or node pointer. That state is private to the iterator. This separation allows you to supply many different concrete iterators for the same aggregate, each with its own traversal strategy. A frequent misconception is thinking the aggregate must perform traversal. In fact, traversal logic belongs in the iterator; the aggregate's responsibility is storage and providing iterator instances. Keeping responsibilities separate keeps code easier to test and extend. Iterator and Aggregate: the two roles means iterator: defines traversal. aggregate: creates iterators and hides storage. concrete pairs implement the contract.. In practical terms, interface contracts and the concrete partners that implement them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Two collaborating roles
keyIdea.text: Iterator: defines traversal. Aggregate: creates iterators and hides storage. Concrete pairs implement the contract.

Iterator Interface
hasNext(), next(), optional remove()
  • hasNext signals whether more elements are available.
  • next returns the next element and advances iterator state.
  • remove, if supported, allows safe removal through the iterator.
Aggregate Interface
iterator() or createIterator()

  • Keeps storage private; clients never access internal arrays or nodes directly.
  • Can offer multiple iterator factories for different traversal strategies.
Concrete Aggregate
Implements the aggregate interface and returns a suitable iterator instance.
Concrete Iterator
Maintains traversal position and accesses elements through aggregate methods.
Client

screens.title: Java's Iterator: hasNext, next, remove
screens.subtitle: What each method must do and safety expectations

narration.text: Java's java. util. Iterator interface is the concrete expression of the pattern in the platform. The two essential methods are hasNext and next. hasNext returns true when the iterator can still produce elements. next returns the next element and advances internal state; it must throw NoSuchElementException if called when no elements remain. The optional remove method, if implemented, removes the last element returned by next from the underlying collection. Implementing remove requires careful coordination with the aggregate so internal indices or links remain correct. A common pitfall is modifying the underlying collection directly while an iterator is active; many Java collections detect structural changes and throw ConcurrentModificationException to surface the error early. When designing custom iterators consider whether to support remove or to throw UnsupportedOperationException. If you need concurrent modification, prefer concurrent collections from java. util. concurrent or synchronize access. Understanding these method contracts ensures your iterators behave predictably in client code and integrate cleanly with Java's for-each syntax when paired with Iterable. Java's Iterator: hasNext, next, remove means hasnext and next form the traversal contract; next must throw nosuchelementexception at the end. remove is optional and must be implemented carefully.. In practical terms, what each method must do and safety expectations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Method contracts
keyIdea.text: hasNext and next form the traversal contract; next must throw NoSuchElementException at the end. remove is optional and must be implemented carefully.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Iterator API
Method descriptions
  • hasNext(): boolean — checks if more elements exist.
  • next(): E — returns next element, advances state, throws NoSuchElementException if empty.
  • remove(): void — optional; removes last returned element through iterator semantics.
Misconception
Calling next without checking hasNext is a runtime error. Always check hasNext or handle NoSuchElementException.
Code sketch
<!-- Example: iterator loop sketch -->
Iterator<Book> it = library.createIterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
  Book b = it.next();
  System.out.println(b);
}

// If next() is called now, it should throw NoSuchElementException
The code above illustrates safe iteration using hasNext, and shows the contract that next must enforce.

screens.title: Implementing Library and Book (aggregate)
screens.subtitle: A concrete aggregate that returns an iterator

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete aggregate: a Library that holds Book objects. The aggregate keeps an internal list and exposes methods the iterator will use, such as getBook(int index) and getNumberOfBooks(). Importantly, the Library implements Iterable so it can return an iterator for enhanced for-loops. The addBook method manages storage without exposing the underlying collection. The iterator factory method, createIterator or iterator, returns a new LibraryIterator configured with this Library instance. This keeps traversal details outside clients. As an example, adding and returning books requires only the aggregate methods; the iterator will call those methods instead of accessing the collection directly. A common mistake is to expose the underlying list through a getter. Resist providing a direct reference; instead, offer controlled accessors the iterator can use. Practicing this separation simplifies testing: you can test LibraryIterator independently by giving it a small Library instance and verifying traversal order and end behavior. Implementing Library and Book (aggregate) means aggregate provides controlled accessors and a factory for iterators; it should not expose internal collections directly.. In practical terms, a concrete aggregate that returns an iterator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Aggregate design
keyIdea.text: Aggregate provides controlled accessors and a factory for iterators; it should not expose internal collections directly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Library Aggregate
Explanation
The Library stores Book objects and exposes addBook, getBook, and getNumberOfBooks. It implements Iterable so it can be used with the enhanced for-loop by returning an iterator instance.
Design tip
Keep accessors minimal and targeted for iterator use to maintain encapsulation.
Code excerpt
<!-- Library: key methods -->
class Library implements BookCollection, Iterable<Book> {
  private List<Book> books = new ArrayList<>();
  public void addBook(Book book) { books.add(book); }
  public Book getBook(int index) { return books.get(index); }
  public int getNumberOfBooks() { return books.size(); }
  public Iterator<Book> createIterator() { return new LibraryIterator(this); }
  @Override public Iterator<Book> iterator() { return createIterator(); }
}
This excerpt shows the aggregate methods the iterator relies on rather than exposing the list directly.

screens.title: LibraryIterator and safe iteration
screens.subtitle: Keeping iteration state and enforcing contracts

narration.text: The Concrete Iterator keeps traversal state and implements hasNext, next, and optionally remove. In the LibraryIterator the iterator holds a reference to the Library and a position index starting at zero. hasNext checks whether position is less than the library's count. next retrieves the book at the current position and then increments the position. If next is called when no elements remain, the iterator throws NoSuchElementException — this explicit exception prevents silent errors. If remove is not practical, the iterator can throw UnsupportedOperationException, which is an explicit contract clients can rely on. Another practical concern is coordinating iterator state with removals: if remove is supported, the iterator must update its index or node references safely so subsequent calls behave correctly. Writing tests that iterate over an empty library and over a populated library will confirm the iterator's edge-case behavior. This focused iterator keeps traversal logic in one place and leaves storage and mutation to the aggregate. LibraryIterator and safe iteration means iterator stores traversal state and enforces method contracts. throw nosuchelementexception when exhausted and decide on remove semantics clearly.. In practical terms, keeping iteration state and enforcing contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Iterator internals
keyIdea.text: Iterator stores traversal state and enforces method contracts. Throw NoSuchElementException when exhausted and decide on remove semantics clearly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › LibraryIterator
Iterator behavior
  • Maintain a position index or node reference.
  • hasNext uses aggregate.getNumberOfBooks() to decide.
  • next uses aggregate.getBook(position) then increments position.
  • Throw NoSuchElementException when next is called with no elements left.
Code excerpt
<!-- LibraryIterator core -->
class LibraryIterator implements Iterator<Book> {
  private Library library;
  private int position = 0;
  public LibraryIterator(Library library) { this.library = library; }
  @Override public boolean hasNext() { return position < library.getNumberOfBooks(); }
  @Override public Book next() {
    if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
    return library.getBook(position++);
  }
  @Override public void remove() {
    throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Remove not supported");
  }
}
Test the iterator on empty and non-empty libraries to confirm correct exceptions and traversal order.

screens.title: Iterable and the enhanced for-loop
screens.subtitle: How implementing Iterable enables for-each syntax

narration.text: Java's enhanced for-loop is convenient because it relies on the Iterable contract. If a class implements java. lang. Iterable and returns a java. util. Iterator from iterator(), the compiler translates the for-each construct into iterator-based code. Implementing Iterable on a custom aggregate like Library means clients can write for (Book b : library) and get familiar, concise syntax without caring about the iterator object. Behind the scenes the for-each loop calls iterator(), uses hasNext and next, and handles the loop lifecycle. This makes your aggregate integrate smoothly with the language. However, do not confuse Iterable with thread-safety: using for-each does not make iteration safe in multi-threaded contexts. If the underlying collection changes structurally during iteration, iterators from standard collections will usually throw ConcurrentModificationException. When you implement Iterable, ensure iterator() returns a fresh iterator instance so multiple loops can run independently. This small integration step improves ergonomics and encourages consistent traversal across client code. Iterable and the enhanced for-loop means implement iterable to allow enhanced for-loops; iterator() must return a new iterator instance for independent traversals.. In practical terms, how implementing iterable enables for-each syntax. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Iterable convenience
keyIdea.text: Implement Iterable to allow enhanced for-loops; iterator() must return a new iterator instance for independent traversals.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Iterable & for-each
Why implement Iterable
It lets clients use concise for-each loops while your class still returns a standard iterator. Returning a fresh iterator each call ensures multiple traversals can run concurrently without shared state.
Quick reminder
for-each is syntactic sugar for iterator-based traversal; behavior and safety follow iterator contracts.
Code example
// After Library implements Iterable<Book>
for (Book book : library) {
  System.out.println("Reading: " + book);
}

// Compiler translates this into use of iterator(), hasNext(), next()
Ensure iterator() returns a new iterator instance each call so loops don't interfere with one another.

screens.title: Fail-fast behavior and concurrent modification
screens.subtitle: What fail-fast iterators detect and when to use concurrent collections

narration.text: Many iterators in the Java Collections Framework are fail-fast: they detect structural modifications to the underlying collection after the iterator is created and throw ConcurrentModificationException. The goal is early detection of bugs where one part of code modifies a collection while another part iterates without coordination. This is not a comprehensive thread-safety mechanism; instead it serves as a guardrail during development and debugging. If you expect concurrent mutation, choose explicit synchronization or use concurrent collections designed for safe concurrent traversal. Another option is to design iterators that operate on a snapshot copy of the collection, trading memory for stability. A frequent misconception is assuming fail-fast means thread-safe — it does not. Fail-fast merely surfaces unexpected concurrent or external modifications. When implementing custom iterators, consider how you will detect structural changes: a simple modification counter in the aggregate that iterators capture at creation time is a common approach. If aggregate. modCount differs from the iterator's captured value, next or hasNext can throw the exception. Fail-fast behavior and concurrent modification means fail-fast detects structural changes to prevent inconsistent traversal; use concurrent collections or snapshots for safe multi-threaded iteration.. In practical terms, what fail-fast iterators detect and when to use concurrent collections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fail-fast summary
keyIdea.text: Fail-fast detects structural changes to prevent inconsistent traversal; use concurrent collections or snapshots for safe multi-threaded iteration.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Fail-fast & Concurrency
What fail-fast does
Detects structural changes and throws ConcurrentModificationException to prevent inconsistent iteration and to help find concurrency bugs early.
When to avoid:
  • In heavily concurrent systems; prefer concurrent collections or synchronized access.
  • When snapshot semantics are preferred, return a copy-based iterator instead.
Implementation hint
Maintain a modification counter in the aggregate. Iterators capture it at creation. If it changes during traversal, throw ConcurrentModificationException from next() or hasNext().

screens.title: Custom iterators: traversal strategies
screens.subtitle: Providing forward, reverse, and filtered traversals without exposing storage

narration.text: One of the Iterator pattern's strengths is that an aggregate can provide multiple iterator implementations to support different traversal strategies. For example, a Playlist aggregate can offer ForwardPlaylistIterator and ReversePlaylistIterator or an iterator that filters songs by genre. The client chooses an iterator factory or a parameter that returns the desired iterator without ever learning about the collection type. That enables features like reverse playback, shuffling, or filtered views, implemented as separate iterators. When designing these iterators, keep them small and focused on traversal; let the aggregate perform removal or structural updates where necessary. A filtered iterator can wrap an existing iterator and skip elements that do not match a predicate, or it can be implemented directly by checking elements before returning them. A common misconception is duplicating storage for each traversal; prefer lightweight iterators that reference the aggregate and do not copy data unless snapshot semantics are required. Custom iterators: traversal strategies means provide different concrete iterators for different traversal needs. the client picks a strategy without touching storage code.. In practical terms, providing forward, reverse, and filtered traversals without exposing storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Multiple strategies
keyIdea.text: Provide different concrete iterators for different traversal needs. The client picks a strategy without touching storage code.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Traversal Strategies
Strategy examples
  • Forward iterator: standard sequential order.
  • Reverse iterator: tracks from tail to head or uses index reverse.
  • Filtered iterator: returns only elements matching a condition.
Design pattern
Offer multiple createIterator methods or a single factory that accepts a traversal parameter. Clients remain oblivious to internal storage while gaining flexible traversal options.
Analogy
Like different folders that present the same photos in different orders: the storage is the same, presentation varies.

screens.title: External vs Internal Iterators
screens.subtitle: Who drives the traversal: the client or the collection?

narration.text: Iterators come in two broad flavors: external and internal. External iterators are the familiar java. util. Iterator objects the client controls by calling hasNext and next. The client explicitly steps through elements and decides when to stop. Internal iterators, in contrast, are controlled by the collection: the aggregate takes a callback or consumer and applies it to each element internally, often in a forEach-style method. Internal iteration can be more concise and can enable implementation-specific optimizations, but it gives the collection control of traversal and limits the client's ability to break early or manage iteration state. In Java, streams and forEach consume elements internally. Choose external iterators when you need client-driven control, removal semantics, or to pause traversal. Choose internal iteration when you want concise processing and the aggregate can efficiently manage traversal. A common mistake is applying internal iteration when the client needs to stop mid-way; prefer external iterators in that case. External vs Internal Iterators means external iterators give control to the client via hasnext/next. internal iterators process elements inside the aggregate using callbacks or consumers.. In practical terms, who drives the traversal: the client or the collection?. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Iteration styles
keyIdea.text: External iterators give control to the client via hasNext/next. Internal iterators process elements inside the aggregate using callbacks or consumers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › External vs Internal
External Iterator
Client calls hasNext and next. Use when traversal control, removal, or pausing is needed.
Example: java.util.Iterator used directly or via enhanced for-loop.
Internal Iterator
Aggregate accepts a callback and applies it to each element internally. Use for concise processing and possible optimizations.
Caveat: clients cannot easily stop mid-iteration or manage complex state.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from this chapter

narration.text: Let's recap the essential ideas to remember. First: the Iterator Pattern separates traversal from storage. That separation reduces coupling and lets you change internals without changing clients. Second: the Iterator interface in Java — with hasNext, next, and optional remove — defines clear contracts. next must throw NoSuchElementException when exhausted and remove must be implemented carefully or explicitly disabled. Third: Java's Iterable integrates iterators with the enhanced for-loop; implement iterator() to return a fresh iterator instance. Also remember fail-fast behavior: many standard iterators detect structural modification and throw ConcurrentModificationException to uncover bugs. These concepts together help you design safe, flexible, and maintainable traversal APIs for custom collections. Key Concepts means iterator encapsulates traversal, java defines standard contracts, and iterable enables ergonomic for-each usage.. In practical terms, three compact reminders from this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Recall
keyIdea.text: Iterator encapsulates traversal, Java defines standard contracts, and Iterable enables ergonomic for-each usage.

Summary takeaway

Design iterators to centralize traversal, enforce contracts for safety, and integrate with Iterable for ergonomic client code.

narration.text: Keep these practical tips at hand when implementing iterators. First, capture a modification counter in the aggregate and check it inside the iterator if you want fail-fast detection. Second, prefer returning fresh iterator instances from iterator() so separate traversals don't interfere. Third, keep iterator responsibilities limited to traversal and element access; let the aggregate manage complex mutations. Fourth, decide explicitly whether remove is supported; throwing UnsupportedOperationException is acceptable and clear. Fifth, for concurrent environments use the concurrent collection types or snapshot copies rather than relying on fail-fast behavior for correctness. These pragmatic choices will help your iterators be robust, predictable, and easy to reason about in both single-threaded and multi-threaded contexts. What to Remember means use modification counters, return fresh iterators, limit iterator responsibilities, and choose thread-safe strategies when needed..
